newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's next president inherits oil might.
newsitem.headline: Iran's next president inherits oil might.

text.p: Mohammad Khatami's fortunes as Iran's next president will be swayed by New York and London oil trading floors as much as domestic politics and foreign affairs.

Iran's economy and the social welfare of its 60 million people are heavily dependent on the huge oilfields of southern Iran which make the Islamic republic the world's third largest oil exporter behind Saudi Arabia and Norway.

Iran's daily crude exports of 2.5 million barrels bring in $18 billion a year in petrodollars paid mainly by customers in Asia and Europe which accounts for some 40 percent of state budget revenue and more than 80 percent of total export revenue.

Without the oil, and the related petrochemical sector, the second largest member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) would be reduced to relying on exports of luxury Persian carpets and pistachio nuts.

The country's strategic importance is heightened by its ownership of 7.5 percent of total world oil reserves and 15 percent of global gas deposits. Iran is also a potential transit route for growing oil and natural gas exports from the former republics of the Soviet Union to the West.

Despite attempts to reduce dependency on oil, the price of crude -- now largely set by international oil firms, traders and speculators -- will be critical to the performance of the economy under Khatami.

Oil prices have been slowly recovering since late 1994 but analysts forecast that they are unlikely to surge because of rising production from states outside OPEC and the partial return of Iraq to world markets.
Tehran's 1997-1998 budget is based on an average price for the country's oil export grades of around $17.50 a barrel. Iran Heavy crude was trading at $17 in Europe on Thursday.

Iran's oil sector is the focus of the United States' trade and investment embargo against Tehran, culminating in the 1996 Iran Libya Sanctions Act which threatens penalties against non-U.S. firms investing in Iran's oil sector.
Oil is not just vital to the local economy but is also a fierce political battlefield.
"Oil is politics and politics is oil," said a manager at the state-owned National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC).
Washington has targeted the oil sector to isolate Iran which it accuses of sponsoring international terrorism and seeking weapons of mass destruction -- charges which Tehran denies.

U.S. President Bill Clinton has banned U.S. firms from developing Iranian oilfields, stopped the multi-billion dollar oil trade between NIOC and American business and pressured international firms and banks not to invest in oil and gas projects which Tehran has opened to foreign investors.

Iran produces 3.6 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude but has reopened its energy sector to foreign investment for the first time since its 1979 revolution in order to maintain capacity and its export potential in the next decade.
Khatami, who is due to take the oath of office on Monday, comes to power at a crucial juncture in Tehran's sanctions standoff with Washington.
NIOC has reached advanced negotiations with France's Total SA and the Anglo-Dutch Royal Dutch Shell Group for a $3.5 billion development of the giant offshore South Pars gas field.
Total, backed by the French government and already a partner in the Sirri oil and gas fields off Iran's southern shore, has defied U.S. extra-territorial legislation.

Khatami's focus on the energy sector is expected to be a programme to expand the added-value petrochemical sector, getting gas export projects off the ground and securing stakes in foreign oil refineries.
